title: CSV Line Parser
description: Split one CSV line into fields, honouring quoted fields, escaped quotes and commas inside quotes.
statement:
A data import has to read one line of a CSV file without splitting on the commas inside quoted fields. Write `parse_csv_line(line)` that returns the fields of the line as a list of strings.

- Fields are separated by commas. Spaces belong to the field and are not trimmed: `a, b` gives `["a", " b"]`.
- A field may be wrapped in double quotes. A comma inside the quotes does not split, `""` inside the quotes stands for one `"`, and the wrapping quotes are not part of the value.
- Empty fields are kept: `a,,b` has three fields, and an empty line is one empty field, `[""]`.
- A quoted field that is never closed raises `ValueError`.
- A quote only ever wraps a whole field: you will not get `ab"c` or `"ab"c`. The line has no newline.

**Examples**

```python
parse_csv_line('name,age,city')         # ["name", "age", "city"]
parse_csv_line('"Smith, Jo",42,')       # ["Smith, Jo", "42", ""]
parse_csv_line('"She said ""hi""",x')   # ['She said "hi"', "x"]
parse_csv_line('a,"b')                  # raises ValueError
```
tests: assert parse_csv_line(" a , b ") == [" a ", " b "]
hints: A comma only splits a field when you are not inside quotes, so at every point you need to know whether you are inside a quoted field. Read the line from left to right and keep that in mind.

At the start of a field, look at its first character. If it is a double quote, read up to the closing quote, treating two quotes in a row as one literal quote; otherwise read up to the next comma. Then you are at a comma or at the end of the line.

After a comma there is always another field, possibly empty: `a,` has two. A closing quote is a quote that is not followed by another quote; reaching the end of the line before you find one is the `ValueError`.
explanation:
**The idea.** Walk the line with an index and read one field at a time. At the start of a field look at its first character: a quote means a quoted field; anything else is a plain field that runs up to the next comma. After a field you are either at the end of the line or on a comma, and a comma always means that one more field follows, even an empty one.

**Quoted fields.** Look for the next quote. If there is none, the field never closes: raise `ValueError`. If that quote is followed by another quote, the pair is one literal `"`, so keep reading. Otherwise it is the closing quote. Searching with `str.find` jumps over long stretches of ordinary text instead of looking at every character.

**Why the empty cases work.** The loop always produces a field before it checks for the end of the line, so an empty line gives `[""]` and `a,` gives `["a", ""]`. Splitting on every comma first and repairing the pieces afterwards is the usual trap: commas inside quotes are easy to get wrong that way.

**Complexity.** O(n) time and space. Cutting the line down by one character at a time copies the rest of the line on every step and is O(n²).

**Usual mistakes.** Taking the last `""` before the end of the line for a closing quote (`"abc""` is unterminated), trimming spaces, and treating `""""` as an empty field instead of a single quote.

**Follow-up.** Real CSV allows line breaks inside quoted fields, so a parser has to read across lines. Python's `csv` module does that, and lets you choose the delimiter and the quote character.
